aggregate.text: A crumb of soil: grains of sand, silt and clay stuck together by humus, microbial gums, fine roots and fungal threads.

browns.text: Dry, woody compost materials rich in carbon, such as autumn leaves, straw, cardboard and wood chips.

clay.text: Mineral grains smaller than 0.002 mm: flat plates that are sticky when wet and hold water and nutrients on their huge surface.

compaction.text: Soil pressed dense, by feet, machines or digging, so that its big pores are squeezed out and water, air and roots can't get through.

compost.text: Plant and kitchen waste rotted down by microbes in a heap, until it is dark and crumbly. It feeds soil life and adds organic matter.

cover-crop.text: A crop grown for the soil rather than to eat: it covers, roots and feeds the bed between food crops. Also called a green manure.

crumb.text: Rounded, soft aggregates from rice- to pea-sized, with big pores between them: the structure most plants grow best in.

earthworm-casts.text: What earthworms leave behind after eating soil and dead leaves: little heaps of soil richer in nutrients and stronger in crumb than the soil around.

food-web.text: Everything that lives in soil and who eats whom: plants and dead plants at the bottom, then bacteria and fungi, then the protozoa, nematodes, mites and worms that eat them.

fungi.text: Soil organisms that grow as fine threads, breaking down tough woody matter, binding crumbs, and in partnership with roots bringing them water and phosphorus.

greens.text: Soft, fresh compost materials rich in nitrogen, such as grass clippings, kitchen scraps and manure.

infiltration.text: Water soaking into soil from the surface. When rain falls faster than a soil's infiltration rate, the rest pools or runs off.

jar-test.text: Shaking soil in a jar of water and measuring the layers as they settle, to find its texture.

lime.text: Ground limestone, spread to raise the pH of an acid soil. Dolomitic lime adds magnesium as well as calcium.

loam.text: A soil with a balanced mix of sand, silt and clay, roughly 40, 40 and 20 parts in a hundred, in which none takes over.

minerals.text: The rock part of soil: sand, silt and clay.

mulch.text: A layer laid on top of the soil, such as straw, leaves, wood chips or compost, to keep water in, shield the surface and feed soil life.

nematodes.text: Tiny worms, mostly harmless, that graze bacteria and fungi and release nitrogen. A few kinds eat roots.

nitrate.text: The form most soil nitrogen ends up in. Plants take it up readily, but it isn't held by clay or humus and washes out with water.

no-dig.text: Growing without turning the soil over: compost is laid on top and soil life works it in, which keeps crumbs and fungi intact.

organic-matter.text: Anything in soil that was alive: roots, leaves, dead creatures, and the humus they rot down to.

pores.text: The spaces between soil grains and crumbs, shared between water and air. About half of a good soil.

protozoa.text: Single-celled hunters in soil water that eat bacteria and release the spare nitrogen as ammonium, by the roots.

sand.text: Mineral grains from 2 mm down to 0.05 mm: gritty, quick to drain, holding little.

silt.text: Mineral grains from 0.05 mm down to 0.002 mm: smooth and floury, and prone to crusting when bare.

slake-test.text: Setting a dry clod in water to see whether its crumbs hold together or fall apart.

soil-test.text: A lab analysis of a soil sample, giving its pH, main nutrients and often its organic matter and cation exchange capacity.

structure.text: How a soil's grains are put together: in crumbs, in plates or blocks, or loose. Unlike texture, it can be changed.

texture.text: A soil's mix of sand, silt and clay, named from the texture triangle. It can't be changed in a season.

tilth.text: A gardener's word for how good a soil is to work and plant into: crumbly, moist, easy to dig or rake.
